headline: Scientists study special jungle penguins in New Zealand

sentences.text: Researchers look at a special bird in New Zealand.

Researchers in New Zealand are studying a special forest bird known as the tawaki.
This creature features bright yellow lines near its eyes and lives deep in dense trees.
Scientists spent four days trying to catch a female bird inside a burrow on an island.
The smart animal used multiple tunnels to escape from its pursuers during the study.
Long-term counts have mapped twelve hundred nests across nine fjords over twelve years.
Experts discovered that the total population is roughly three times larger than past reports suggested.
Before their yearly feather change, these birds make a long trip toward the southern region to feed.
Scientists are studying a unique water bird known for its distinct yellow head marks and tree-living habits.
A research team spent four days trying to capture a female bird on an island to retrieve data from a device.
The smart animal avoided researchers by digging multiple escape tunnels around its underground home.
Over the past twelve years, twelve hundred nests have been mapped across nine fjords by the project.
Survey results indicate that the total population is roughly three times larger than earlier estimates suggested.
Unlike most related species, these birds do not breed in colonies and prefer single burrows in the rainforest.
Before undergoing their yearly feather change, these birds undertake a long trip toward the sub-Antarctic region to feed.
Researchers in New Zealand are working to understand a unique water bird known for its distinct yellow eyebrows and forest home.
Catching these elusive animals proves very difficult, as shown when a team spent four days trying to corner a female on an island.
The smart creature successfully avoided people by digging multiple exit tunnels beneath its underground nest.
The project has mapped twelve hundred nests across nine fjords, revealing a population roughly three times larger than past estimates.
Unlike most related animals, these birds never breed in groups, choosing instead to build single burrows deep within thick rainforest areas.
Before undergoing their yearly feather change, these thin birds undertake a massive return trip toward the sub-Antarctic region.
This baffling journey makes little sense because local food supplies around the breeding area are abundant in December.
Experts believe the birds follow an ancient instinct to feed where other crested penguin species gather.
